presentingComplaint: New-onset right-sided temporal headache with scalp tenderness and jaw pain on chewing for 3 weeks
history: A 73-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of a new, persistent right temporal headache that is unlike any prior headache. She reports tenderness of the scalp when combing her hair and aching in the jaw muscles after a few minutes of chewing that resolves with rest (jaw claudication). Over the same period she has had bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness worst in the mornings, low-grade malaise, fatigue and about 3 kg of unintentional weight loss. Two days ago she experienced a transient episode of blurring and 'greying out' of vision in the right eye lasting a few minutes (amaurosis fugax). No prior headache disorder. PMH: hypertension, hypothyroidism. No visual loss previously. Non-smoker.
examination: Alert and oriented. Tender, thickened, nodular and pulseless right superficial temporal artery on palpation; scalp tenderness over the temporal region. Fundoscopy currently normal (no pallid disc swelling at this visit). Proximal shoulder-girdle tenderness with restricted active abduction from stiffness. No focal neurological deficit, neck supple, no meningism. Peripheral pulses and cardiovascular exam otherwise normal; no carotid or subclavian bruit.

labs.hemoglobin: 10.8 g/dL (normochromic normocytic anaemia of chronic disease)

imaging: Temporal artery colour Doppler ultrasound shows a non-compressible 'halo sign' (hypoechoic circumferential wall thickening) of the right temporal artery. No large-vessel involvement on limited exam; MR/CT angiography or PET can be considered to assess for aortic/large-vessel involvement.
citations: Harrison 22e — The Vasculitis Syndromes (Giant Cell Arteritis and Polymyalgia Rheumatica)
contraindications: High-dose glucocorticoids: caution in poorly controlled hypertension, diabetes and osteoporosis risk — start bone protection and gastric prophylaxis
Do NOT delay steroids awaiting temporal artery biopsy when visual symptoms are present — sight-threatening emergency
edgeCases: Vision loss (anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy) can be sudden, painless and irreversible; amaurosis fugax is a red-flag warning of impending permanent loss requiring emergency high-dose steroids
ESR/CRP can occasionally be normal in a small minority of biopsy-proven GCA, so normal inflammatory markers do not exclude it when clinical suspicion is high
Biopsy may be negative due to skip lesions — a negative biopsy does not exclude GCA
expectedMaiK: Classic giant cell arteritis in a woman over 50 with new temporal headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, PMR-type stiffness and markedly raised ESR/CRP; the transient monocular visual loss makes this a sight-threatening emergency. Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and arrange urgent temporal artery biopsy/ultrasound — do not wait for the biopsy.
expectedNextQuestions: Any jaw or tongue claudication, and any episodes of transient or persistent visual loss / double vision?
New headache in someone over 50 with proximal girdle stiffness suggestive of polymyalgia rheumatica?
expectedInvestigations: Temporal artery biopsy (and/or temporal artery Doppler ultrasound for the halo sign)

investigations: Temporal artery biopsy / temporal artery ultrasound
